common_name: Cristata Moss Rose (Chapeau de Napoleon, Crested Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cristata is a moss rose sport with distinctive crested, mossy sepals resembling a folded hat.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Cristata, popularly called Chapeau de Napoleon for its curious buds, bears large, fragrant, clear pink double blooms enclosed in sepals so heavily crested and fringed with green, moss-like growth that unopened buds resemble a tiny folded tricorn hat, a whimsical trait unique among old roses. Like other Centifolia-derived roses it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Salet Moss Rose (Repeat-Blooming Pink Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Salet is a repeat-blooming moss rose, an advantage over most once-blooming moss cultivars.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Salet bears fragrant, clear pink double blooms surrounded by soft, resinous, moss-textured sepals that release a distinctive balsam scent when touched, a hallmark of moss roses, and unlike most of its class it reliably repeats bloom through the season rather than flowering just once. Its balance of the classic mossy old-rose look with genuine repeat flowering has made it one of the most practical moss roses for a modern mixed border. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after each bloom flush.

common_name: William Lobb Moss Rose (Purple-Magenta Fading to Lavender-Grey)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; William Lobb is a tall, vigorous moss rose whose flower color shifts dramatically as blooms age.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the tall, arching canes benefit from support or a spot where they can lean into a fence or shrub. William Lobb opens deep purple-magenta double blooms that fade through smoky mauve to a striking lavender-grey as they age, so a single bush shows several colors at once, all carried on brownish, heavily mossed sepals with the characteristic balsam fragrance of the class. Like most moss roses it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Henri Martin Moss Rose (Vivid Crimson-Red Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Henri Martin is a vigorous, arching moss rose with vivid crimson-red blooms.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Henri Martin bears loose, semi-double, vivid crimson-red blooms with a light, sweet fragrance, opening from lightly mossed buds on a vigorous, arching shrub that can be trained as a short climber against a fence or pillar. Like most moss roses it blooms just once, in a spectacular flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Comtesse de Murinais Moss Rose (White-Blush Fragrant Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Comtesse de Murinais bears pale blush-white blooms fading to white on a tall moss rose shrub.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Comtesse de Murinais opens from pink-tinted buds heavily wrapped in green, resinous moss into large, fully double blooms that fade to a soft blush-white, carrying a strong, sweet fragrance typical of the class. Its tall, upright growth and pale, refined color have made it a favorite for the back of an antique rose border. Like other moss roses it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, and is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Alfred de Dalmas Moss Rose (Repeat-Blooming Pale Pink Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Alfred de Dalmas, also sold as Mousseline, is a compact, repeat-blooming moss rose.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Alfred de Dalmas, also sold under the name Mousseline, bears soft pale pink, cupped, double blooms lightly touched with moss on the sepals, opening on a compact, well-behaved shrub that fits a smaller garden more readily than many taller moss roses. It reliably repeats bloom through the season rather than flowering just once, an unusual and valuable trait for the moss rose class. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after each bloom flush.

common_name: Nuits de Young Moss Rose (Darkest Maroon-Purple Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Nuits de Young is among the darkest-colored moss roses, nearly black-purple.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Nuits de Young bears small, semi-double blooms in the darkest maroon-purple of any commonly grown moss rose, verging on black in bud and accented by contrasting golden stamens, with dark brownish moss covering the sepals and a light, spicy fragrance. Its unusually dark, dramatic color has made it a favorite among old-rose collectors seeking something beyond the typical pink palette. Like other moss roses it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, and is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy.

common_name: Madame Pierre Oger Rose (Pale Pink-and-Cream Cupped Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Pierre Oger is a repeat-blooming Bourbon rose whose delicate cupped blooms deepen in color with more sun.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Madame Pierre Oger bears delicate, cupped, double blooms in pale cream-pink that deepen to a richer rose-pink with stronger sun exposure, opening on a graceful, upright Bourbon shrub with the strong, sweet fragrance typical of the class. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a genuine advantage of Bourbon roses over many once-blooming old garden rose classes. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Boule de Neige Rose (Snowball White Double Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Boule de Neige is a repeat-blooming white Bourbon rose whose buds resemble small snowballs.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Boule de Neige, French for 'snowball,' bears crimson-tinted buds that open into fully double, pure white blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance, the round, densely petaled form giving the flower its snowball nickname. It repeats bloom reliably through the growing season and tolerates a bit more shade than many other roses, useful in a border that isn't in full sun all day. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Variegata di Bologna Rose (Striped Red-White-Purple Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Variegata di Bologna bears dramatically striped red-purple-and-white blooms, mostly on a single strong spring flush.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy support, since the vigorous canes can be trained as a short climber. Variegata di Bologna bears large, fully double blooms boldly striped in raspberry-red and purple over a white ground, an eye-catching, painterly pattern among Bourbon roses, with a strong, sweet fragrance. Unlike some repeat-blooming Bourbons it flowers mainly in a single dramatic spring flush with only light rebloom later, so plant it where its once-yearly show provides maximum impact. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.

common_name: Honorine de Brabant Rose (Striped Pink-and-Purple Blush Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Honorine de Brabant is a striped, repeat-blooming Bourbon rose that tolerates more shade than most roses.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Honorine de Brabant tolerates more shade than most roses, blooming reasonably well with only a half-day of sun. Its large, cupped, blush-pink blooms are softly striped and speckled with lavender-purple, a subtler pattern than the boldly striped Bourbon roses, carrying a strong, sweet fragrance and repeating well through the growing season. Its shade tolerance and repeat bloom make it a versatile choice for a spot too shaded for most other roses. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Celine Forestier Rose (Pale Yellow Climbing Noisette Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence; Celine Forestier is a fragrant, repeat-blooming, pale yellow climbing Noisette rose well suited to the Gulf South heat.

directions: Plant own-root stock in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence. Celine Forestier bears pale lemon-yellow, quartered double blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening in flushes nearly continuously through the warm season on a vigorous climbing Noisette that, like other roses in its class, thrives on the heat and humidity of the Gulf South that stresses many modern climbers. Its soft color and repeat bloom make it a graceful choice for an arbor, porch post, or fence. Prune lightly after each bloom flush and train canes horizontally along the support to maximize flowering side shoots.

common_name: Madame Alfred Carriere Rose (White-Blush Vigorous Climbing Noisette Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis or fence; Madame Alfred Carriere is a vigorous, cold-hardier climbing Noisette that tolerates some shade.

directions: Plant own-root stock in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis, wall, or fence. Madame Alfred Carriere bears large, fragrant, white blooms tinted with soft blush-pink, opening in flushes almost continuously through the warm season on an exceptionally vigorous, cold-hardier climbing Noisette that reaches greater heights than many others in its class and tolerates a north-facing or partly shaded wall better than most roses. Its combination of toughness, shade tolerance, and repeat bloom has made it one of the most widely planted antique climbers. Prune lightly after each bloom flush and train canes horizontally along the support to maximize flowering side shoots.

planting.note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence; Crepuscule is a warm apricot-orange climbing Noisette especially popular in Gulf South and Australian gardens.

directions: Plant own-root stock in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence. Crepuscule, French for 'twilight,' bears warm apricot-orange double blooms that soften to buff-yellow as they age, opening in flushes nearly continuously through the warm season with a light, sweet fragrance, and its heat tolerance has made it especially popular in Gulf South, Bermuda, and Australian gardens where it thrives on long, hot summers. Its thornless-to-nearly-thornless canes are easy to train along a fence or arbor. Prune lightly after each bloom flush and train canes horizontally along the support to maximize flowering side shoots.

common_name: Desprez a Fleur Jaune Rose (Buff-Apricot Historic Climbing Noisette Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence; Desprez a Fleur Jaune, introduced in 1830, was one of the first yellow-toned Noisette roses.

directions: Plant own-root stock in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence. Introduced in France in 1830, Desprez a Fleur Jaune bears buff-apricot to soft yellow blooms with an unusually rich, fruity fragrance often compared to ripe bananas or peaches, opening in flushes through the warm season on a vigorous climbing Noisette that was among the earliest roses to introduce yellow tones into the class. Its heat tolerance suits it well to Gulf South conditions where many modern roses struggle. Prune lightly after each bloom flush and train canes horizontally along the support to maximize flowering side shoots.
